result: Zebrafish contain diverse types of cilia with variable lengths across different organs and cell types, ranging from ~0.49 μm in epidermal cells to ~25.46 μm in crista, with most cells containing single cilia while specialized cells form multicilia.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors unveil the surprising breadth of intraflagellar transport speed among differing organs,' implicitly accepting the diversity of cilia. Reviewer 2 notes 'They observe striking differences in cilia lengths...in different cilia types.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities can differ markedly in cilia of different cell types' and praises 'the experiments were carefully done and results are generally convincing.'

result: Ift88-GFP can functionally substitute for endogenous Ift88, as demonstrated by rescue of ovl mutant phenotypes including body curvature defects, ciliogenesis defects, and survival to adulthood.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this result without challenge. Reviewer 2 states 'They elucidate that IFT88-GFP...can substitute for endogenous IFT88 in promoting ciliogenesis' as a strength. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'demonstrated that ectopically expressed Ift88-GFP...was able to sustain the normal development of and the cilia formation in ovl-/- zebrafish...suggesting a full function of the exogenous protein.' No concerns are raised about this functional validation.

result: IFT speeds vary significantly across different cell types in zebrafish, with longer cilia exhibiting faster IFT speeds. A strong positive correlation exists between cilia length and both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this correlation. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'link this to cell type-specific differences in cilia length.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The authors have robustly shown that the cilia length and IFT train speeds are highly variable between organs and have a strong correlation.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'IFT velocities in different types of cells are positively correlated with inherent ciliary lengths' and states 'the experiments were carefully done and results are generally convincing.'

result: IFT speeds are intrinsic to cell types rather than dependent on cilia growth phase or developmental stage, as demonstrated by comparable IFT velocities in cilia of similar length within the same cell type at different developmental stages.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'specific IFT velocities are intrinsic to cell types' as one of the key demonstrations. Reviewer 2 implicitly accepts this by noting the correlation is with 'cell types' rather than developmental factors. No reviewer challenges this interpretation of the data.

result: IFT speed variation is not explained by common regulatory factors including motor selection (Kif17, Kif3b), BBSome proteins (Bbs4), tubulin modifications (glycylation via Ttll3, glutamylation via Ttll6/Ccp5), or ATP concentration differences.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these negative results. Reviewer 2 notes 'They make some interesting findings in mutants with disrupted function of kinesin-2, BBSome and tubulin modifying enzymes which are interesting to compare with cilia studies in other model organisms.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Depletion of proteins such as Bbs4, Ttll3, Ttll6, and Ccp5 did not substantially alter the IFT velocities' without challenging the findings. These exclusions strengthen the novelty of the subsequent train size hypothesis.

result: Longer cilia (ear crista) contain larger IFT particles compared to shorter cilia (spinal cord), as measured by STED super-resolution microscopy showing significantly larger particle sizes in crista versus spinal cord cilia.
evaluation: This is the most contentious result. Reviewer 2 states 'the claim that the cilia length (and IFT velocity) in different organs is different due to difference in the sizes of IFT trains is based on weak evidence. This is based on a marginal difference of IFT train sizes they observe between cilia of crista and spinal cord in immunofluorescence experiments (Fig. 5C). Inferring that this minor difference is key to the striking difference in cilia length and IFT velocity is too bold.' Reviewer 3 notes 'IFT velocities are positively correlated with the size of IFT trains' but also states 'the proposed model is reasonable, it is largely based on correlations.'

result: Reducing Ift88 levels by morpholino knockdown decreases IFT particle size and number, slows IFT speed, and results in shorter cilia, demonstrating a relationship between IFT particle size and transport velocity.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the data but question the mechanistic interpretation. Reviewer 2 states 'Disruption (or reduced number) of IFTB1 complex could indeed lead to IFT trains not being formed properly...However, this does not directly imply that under wild-type conditions, cilia in spinal cord have poorly formed slightly shorter IFT trains...Such a claim would require much stronger evidence.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The effects of anti-sense RNA-induced Ift88 downregulation on IFT and ciliary length are artificial. It is unclear whether the levels of one or more IFT components are indeed regulated to control IFT train sizes and ciliary lengths in physiological conditions.'

result: The authors propose that IFT particle/train size is related to IFT speed, and that longer cilia form larger IFT trains for more effective cargo transportation, representing a mechanism for cilia length regulation.
evaluation: This central hypothesis receives mixed evaluation. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the central hypothesis of the manuscript, which is cilia length regulation occurs via controlling IFT speed through the modulation of the size of the IFT complex, is supported only with preliminary data and needs stronger evidence' and recommends 'the authors to not give too much weight on the hypothesis that IFT train velocity is determined by the size of IFT trains.' Reviewer 2 also notes 'if IFT train speeds directly correlate with size of IFT train, the authors should be able to see this within the same cilia...This is not apparent from the movies.' Reviewer 3 states 'the proposed model is reasonable, it is largely based on correlations' and notes 'whether IFT velocities are indeed dictated by the size of IFT trains remains to be clarified.'

result: Within crista cilia, anterograde IFT maintains relatively constant speed along the cilium length, while retrograde IFT undergoes slight acceleration when returning to the base.
evaluation: This descriptive finding is not challenged by any reviewer. It represents a technical observation about IFT dynamics that supports the overall characterization of IFT behavior in zebrafish cilia.

result: This study represents the first comparison of IFT in cilia from different organ types within the same organism.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges this as 'a valuable conceptual and technical contribution' and notes the work 'will be of broad interest to researchers in numerous fields.' Reviewer 2 states 'this work develops an exciting new multicellular model organism to study IFT mechanisms' and notes it 'could be an ideal model to study not just the role of IFT in connection with ciliary function but also ciliopathies.' The novelty of the comparative approach is accepted by all reviewers.

result: Background claims about cilia biology, IFT mechanisms, and comparative findings from other model organisms (C. elegans, Chlamydomonas, mouse) that provide context for the study.
evaluation: These are established facts from the literature cited by the authors. Reviewers do not challenge these background claims. However, Reviewer 3 identifies one error: 'In the Discussion section, Kif17 is described as an important motor for IFT in mouse olfactory cilia. In the cited literature (Williams et al., 2014), however, Kif17 is reported to be dispensable for IFT in mouse olfactory cilia. This makes the discussions on Kif17 absurd.'

result: IFT transport speed shows no discernible connection to ciliary motility, as evidenced by comparable IFT speeds in both motile spinal cord cilia and primary cilia of epidermal cells.
evaluation: This inference from the data is not challenged by reviewers. It represents a negative finding that helps define what factors do not explain IFT speed variation.

result: Speculative mechanistic proposals including that longer cilia may have larger IFT pools at the base, recruit higher ratios of motor proteins, or form optimal platforms for efficient transport.
evaluation: These are acknowledged as speculative by the authors and reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes these are 'based on the marginal correlation they observe' and Reviewer 3 states 'the proposed model is reasonable, it is largely based on correlations.' These represent hypotheses for future testing rather than established findings.
